APPLICATION OF Albert Osborn FOR THE ENROLLMENT OF John Osborn IN THE INDIAN SCHOOL AT Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Washington POST-OFFICE ADDRESS OF APPLICANT: Wrangell, Alaska Date of enrollment, Nov. 28, 1918, 19 Term of enrollment, three (3) years. NAME OF PERSON ARRANGING FOR THE TRANSFER: Father brought him Position, APPLICATION FOR ENROLLMENT IN A NONRESERVATION SCHOOL. (For a child not enrolled at an Agency.) For and in consideration of the United States assuming the care, education, and maintenance in the United States Indian School at Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Washington, of John George Osborn, male, 13, I, Albert Osborn, of Wrangell, P.O., State of Alaska, do hereby voluntarily consent and agree to his enrollment in said school for a period of three years, and also oblige and bind myself to abide by all the rules and regulations for Indian schools. I further say that the said child was born at Wrangell, Alaska on Nov. 17, 1906; that the father, Albert Osborn, is a white man, Tribe located at Wrangell Agency; that he left the tribe about 1908; that the mother, Lucy Osborn, was a black Indian of the Tlingit Tribe located at Wrangell Agency, and left the tribe about 1908; that the said child was born and reared in the United States, and now actually resides therein; and that he has attended the following schools:
NAME OF SCHOOL, PUBLIC GOVERNMENT, OR MISSION LOCATED AT DATE OF ENROLLMENT DATE OF DISCHARGE Cause of Discharge GRADE
Public School, Wrangell 1912 1918 Other
Should the child be returned home for one of the vacation periods of this enrollment at my request I further agree to pay all expenses, including round-trip railroad fares, sleeping-car fares, meals, lodging, stage fares, telegraph and telephone messages, and other incidental expenses connected with the visit. I further agree that said pupil shall be returned to the Cushman school on or before the last day of the vacation leave of absence. I further agree to cooperate with the superintendent of the school sufficient money to defray all expenses to be incurred, and should the child fail to return to school at such time as may have been agreed upon by myself and the superintendent of the school, the amount of money paid to the school superintendent, necessary to the return transportation of the child so neglecting to return shall be forfeited to the Government. This 50th day of Nov., 1918 Two witnesses: Lucy M. Smith Al Osborn, father (Parent, guardian, or next of kin.) The law provides: "That no part of this appropriation, or any other appropriation provided for herein except appropriations made pursuant to treaties, shall be used to educate children of less than one-fourth Indian blood whose parents are citizens of the United States and of the State wherein they live and where there are adequate free-school facilities provided and the facilities of the Indian schools are needed for pupils of more than one-fourth Indian blood." EXTRACTS FROM SCHOOL RULES. If the facilities of a school are not needed as provided in the above paragraph, children showing any Indian blood, whose parents live on an Indian reservation, and who if debarred from Government schools could not obtain an education, may be enrolled in the day and boarding schools of their reservation; these children, however, may not be transferred to nonreservation schools without special permission from the Commissioner of Indian Affairs. Before enrolling a pupil superintendents must satisfy themselves whether he has left any other school without permission and whether he has been expelled for cause from any other school. A pupil who has been expelled for cause from any Indian school may be reenrolled in any Indian school only with permission of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs. Attention is invited to Circulars Nos. 1039 and 1044, which must be observed. "The Secretary of the Interior may in his discretion withhold rations, clothing, and other annuities from Indian parents or guardians who refuse or neglect to send or keep their children of proper school age in some school during a reasonable portion of each year." (27 Stat. L., 635. See 2 Dec. Comp., 308.) CASE RECORD. NAME John Osborn Sex Male. Reproduced at the National Archives at Seattle Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., May 6, 1920 Pacific Steamship Co. Seattle, Washington Gentlemen: This office has been advised that a ticket from Seattle to Wrangell, Alaska, has been provided for John Osborn, one of our pupils, by L. M. Churchill, of Wrangell, Alaska. John is planning to take the next boat, which is scheduled to leave Seattle May 11th at 10:00 a.m. Since this ticket has already been paid for, would it be possible for you to mail it to John Osborn, in care of this Office? This would avoid the necessity of his going to Seattle the day before to secure the ticket and having to remain over night in Seattle. However, if it is impossible to mail this ticket to this office, John will call for it May 10th. The only credentials he has is a letter from Mr. L. M. Churchill, of Wrangell, in which he advises that John should call at your Seattle office for the ticket. He also advises that arrangements for the payment of the ticket have already been made by Mr. Churchill. Thanking you for an early response, I am Very respectfully, Clerk in Charge. Rangella Alaska E.H. Hammond. Please turn all my children over to Mrs. Burnes, as I want all to come home together. Their transportation is reserved on the city Seattle about April 6th. Let the boys bring their uniforms and I will pay for them. Father Reborn. April 1-1919. Postal Telegram Rangella Alaska Mr. John Osborn. Mrs. Barnes will be at Cushman next Thursday after you. Gertrude, Albert—and Anna. Get everything ready for next city Seattle. Your father Osborn 3-31-1919 Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Washington April 1, 1919. Mr. Albert Osborn Wrangell, Alaska. My dear Mr. Osborn: I received your telegram and your letter asking that all your children be sent home in care of Mrs. Burnes. As I told you when you left your children here, there would be no objections to your taking the little ones any time you desired. In the case of your son John, however, the loss would be so great that it was decided between you and me that he would not return until June. As soon as I found out that John had written you begging to come home, I wrote you about the matter and urged you not to call for John until he had passed the examinations which will be about the first week in June. After he has passed to grade 7 there will be no objections to his going home for the fishing season. If he leaves before the examinations he will throw away all chances for promotion and will be obliged to go over all the work next year, whether he enters Cushman or a public school. It will be a distinct loss to him and will mean that the school will practically have to go over the same work with your son another year. The boy will lose interest in his studies and will gain a distaste for school which will affect his life most unfavorably. As I told John yesterday, there would be no reason whatsoever, why he should not return to Alaska by June, but if he returns before he has passed examinations it is only fair that you return to the school his board and tuition for the past year, which amounts to $16.66 2/3 a month. Regarding your request to permit the boys to bring home their uniforms with them, we are at liberty to issue uniforms for wearing home only to those pupils who have completed the three years enrollment. I sincerely hope that you will not see fit to take John away from school until after he has obtained every benefit from the instructions he has received. We, the undersigned, respectfully request that leave of absence be granted John Osborn from April 16th to September 5, 1919 to enable him to visit his home. We hereby agree to pay all expenses, including round-trip railroad fares, sleeping-car fares, meals, lodging, stage fares, telegraph and telephone messages, and other incidental expenses connected with the visit. We further agree that said pupil shall be returned to the Cushman school on or before the last day of the leave of absence. We further agree to deposit with the superintendent of the school sufficient money to defray all expenses to be incurred, and should the pupils, or any one of them, fail to return to school at such time as may be agreed upon by the parents or guardian and the superintendent of the school in which the pupils are enrolled, the amount of money remaining with the superintendent, necessary to the return transportation of the pupil or pupils so neglecting to return, shall be forfeited to the Government; provided, however, that in all cases where it can be shown that there were justifiable reasons for the failure of the return of the pupil the forfeiture of the funds shall not take place. If the pupil neglecting to return is from a reservation, the superintendent of the reservation shall certify to the reasons for the nonreturn of the pupil or pupils. If a pupil's home is not on a reservation, then the certificate of some reputable, disinterested citizen of the community may be requested as to the reasons for the nonreturn of the pupil or pupils.
